The Mirror shiner, Notropis spectrunculus, is a small-bodied cyprinid endemic to the upper Tennessee River drainage. Field surveys indicate that individuals typically reach a maximum total length of 7.9 cm [Li = 7.9 cm], a modest size compared to related minnows such as Notropis atherinoides. This ultimate length is achieved over several growing seasons, with the most rapid somatic expansion occurring during the first two years of life. The species is characterized by a relatively compressed body form and a pronounced silvery lateral stripe, features that are consistent among mature individuals. In samples collected from medium-order streams, adults in the upper quartile of the size distribution were routinely observed at this asymptotic length, suggesting that 7.9 cm represents a genuine biological maximum under typical environmental conditions. Growth increments in older specimens become negligible, and analyses of scale annuli confirm that few individuals exceed this threshold even when occupying productive riffle habitats with abundant invertebrate prey.

Puberty in the Mirror shiner is attained at a total length of 3.0 cm [Lp = 3.0 cm], a dimension that corresponds approximately to the end of the first growing season. This length at sexual maturation is derived from otolith-based age assignments, which indicate that most yearling fish have reached or exceeded this size threshold by late spring. At this developmental stage, the body mass of a typical individual is approximately 0.2 g [Wwp = approximately 0.2 g], reflecting the relatively lean body composition of a young cyprinid that has recently completed its first winter. The transition from a juvenile, non-reproductive state to a reproductively competent adult involves the onset of gonadal recrudescence, which is triggered by increasing photoperiod and rising water temperatures. Individuals shorter than 3.0 cm rarely exhibit signs of vitellogenesis or spermatogenesis, confirming that this length marks a reliable and consistent biological milestone for the onset of sexual maturity within wild populations.

Neonates of Notropis spectrunculus emerge from demersal, adhesive eggs at a remarkably small wet weight of 0.00032 g [Wwb = 0.00032 g]. This mass at birth is consistent with an egg diameter of approximately 0.85 mm, as documented in the congener Notropis atherinoides, from which the value is extrapolated. The yolk-sac larva, or prolarva, is entirely dependent on its endogenous yolk reserves during the first few days post-eclosion, a period during which it remains relatively immobile and hidden within the interstitial spaces of gravel substrates. The transition to first exogenous feeding occurs shortly after mouth opening and yolk absorption completion, at which point the larva begins to actively capture small zooplankton such as rotifers and copepod nauplii. This extremely small birth mass imposes a high initial mortality risk, as the tiny larvae are vulnerable to both starvation and predation during the critical early feeding window before they achieve sufficient size to exploit a wider range of prey items.

Maximum adult body mass, or ultimate wet weight, in the Mirror shiner is estimated at 4.1 g [Wwi = 4.1 g], a value derived from a length-weight regression calculated for the species. This asymptotic mass is reached when individuals attain the ultimate total length of 7.9 cm, and it represents the heaviest condition typically recorded among mature, reproductive adults. Body condition varies seasonally, with females often carrying substantial masses of developing oocytes during the spawning period, which can elevate their weight temporarily above the general asymptotic estimate. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a stable temperature of 17.5 °C [T = 17.5 °C], the maximum lifespan of the Mirror shiner has been documented at 1,825 days [am = 1,825 days], which is equivalent to approximately five years. This longevity is relatively modest among North American cyprinids, many of which have lifespans of three to six years, though it is longer than that reported for several congeners that experience higher predation pressure in lotic environments.

Female Mirror shiners exhibit a maximum reproductive output of roughly 0.9 offspring per day [Ri = roughly 0.9 offspring per day] when held at a constant water temperature of 17.5 °C [T = 17.5 °C]. This rate was calculated by observing that gravid females produced approximately 331 eggs over the course of a single 365-day year, a figure that reflects the species' capacity for multiple spawning events within a single reproductive season. Each spawning event yields a clutch of adhesive eggs that are deposited over clean gravel substrates in shallow, fast-flowing riffles. The annual fecundity of approximately 331 eggs per year places the Mirror shiner at the lower end of the fecundity spectrum for its genus, consistent with a life-history strategy that emphasizes moderate parental investment per offspring rather than the production of extremely large numbers of tiny, pelagic eggs. Reproductive activity peaks during late spring and early summer, when day lengths are longest and water temperatures are most favorable for egg development and larval survival.
